summary: It's like the front door of the office is like a keys in there and you walk in and your  day is shredded to bits because you have 15 minutes here and 30 minutes there and then  something else happens and you're pulled off your work and you've got to do something  else and you have 20 minutes on this lunch, then you have something else to do and you  have 15 minutes and someone pulls you aside and asks you this question and before you  know it, it's like it's 5 p.m.  And you look back on your day and you realize that you didn't get anything done.

This is why people choose to do work at home or they might go to the office  but they might go to the office really early in the day or late at night when one's around  or they stick around whenever after everyone's left and they go in on the weekends or they  get work done on the plane or they get work done in the car or in the train because there  are no distractions.

Now, what's interesting is if you listen to all the  places that people talk about doing it, like at home or  in the car or on a plane or late at night or early in  the morning, you don't find managers in meetings.

Another thing you can try is switching from active  communication and collaboration, which is like face-to-face  stuff, tapping people on the shoulder, saying hi to them,  having meetings, and replace that with more passive  models of communication, using things like email, instant  messaging, or collaboration products, things like that.

And I hope that some of these ideas were at least provocative  enough for managers and bosses and business owners and  organizers and people who are in charge of other people to  think about laying off a little bit and giving people  some more time to get some work done.
